lead: DSB-SC sends the two sidebands of an amplitude-modulated wave and removes the carrier. The message rides on a carrier that changes sign with the message, so the envelope is not the message. The receiver must generate a local carrier at exactly the same frequency and phase, multiply, and low-pass filter. This saves the carrier power of plain AM. It is used in colour television chrominance, FM stereo difference channels and some data links.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the AM spectrum and Unit 1 for the Fourier transform and multiplication of signals.

sections.h3: The DSB-SC signal and its spectrum

blocks.text: Let m(t) be the message with bandwidth W in hertz, A_c the carrier amplitude in volts, and f_c the carrier frequency in hertz. DSB-SC is s(t) = A_c m(t) cos(2πf_c t). The message has zero average in the usual case, so m(t) has no DC term.

blocks.where: S(f) is the Fourier transform of s(t); M(f) is the Fourier transform of m(t); A_c is the carrier amplitude in volts; f_c is the carrier frequency in hertz; W is the message bandwidth in hertz.

blocks.text: There is no impulse at ±f_c. The carrier line is suppressed. The occupied band is f_c − W to f_c + W, so the bandwidth is 2W. Use 2 cos A cos B = cos(A−B) + cos(A+B). For a tone m(t) = A_m cos(2πf_m t), the two sidebands are (A_c A_m/2) cos(2π(f_c − f_m)t) and (A_c A_m/2) cos(2π(f_c + f_m)t). Some syllabi call this DSB/SC or double-sideband suppressed carrier. See Chapter 2.3 for the one-sideband case that halves this bandwidth.

A coherent detector multiplies s(t) by a local carrier and low-pass filters the result. With local carrier A_lo cos(2πf_c t), the product is A_c A_lo m(t) cos²(2πf_c t) = (A_c A_lo/2)m(t) + (A_c A_lo/2)m(t) cos(4πf_c t). The low-pass filter removes the double-frequency term.

blocks.where: y(t) is the low-pass filter output in volts; A_c is the received carrier amplitude in volts; A_lo is the local carrier amplitude in volts; m(t) is the message voltage.

blocks.text: With A_lo = 1 and zero phase error, y(t) = (A_c/2)m(t). The output is the baseband message, scaled. The local carrier must match the received carrier in frequency and phase. This is why the method is called coherent detection. Carrier recovery can use a small pilot tone or a Costas loop; the loop locks a local oscillator to the received carrier phase.
An envelope detector does not work here. The DSB-SC wave changes sign, so its envelope is |A_c m(t)|, not m(t). See Chapter 2.5 for the envelope detector used with plain AM.
Let the local carrier be A_lo cos(2πf_c t + φ), where φ is the phase error in radians. After multiplication and low-pass filtering, the output is scaled by cos φ.

blocks.where: φ is the phase difference between the received carrier and the local carrier, in radians; cos φ is the loss factor.

blocks.text: A phase error of 90° gives cos φ = 0, so the output is zero. A phase error of 180° inverts the message. Small phase errors lose little: at 30°, cos φ = 0.866, a 13.4% loss.

Let the local frequency be f_c + Δf, where Δf is the frequency error in hertz. The low-pass output contains m(t) cos(2πΔf t). The message is multiplied by a slow beat. For a tone this gives two tones at f_m ± Δf. Oscillator stability and carrier recovery are therefore part of the receiver design.

figure.caption: The received DSB-SC signal is multiplied by a synchronized local carrier; the low-pass filter removes the double-frequency term and leaves the baseband message. Notice that no envelope detector appears: the local carrier is essential.

spec.title: Coherent DSB-SC detector
spec.aria: The received DSB-SC signal and a local carrier enter a product device; a low-pass filter then gives the baseband output.

examples.question: A 2 V peak, 1 kHz tone modulates a 10 V peak, 100 kHz carrier in DSB-SC. Write the two sideband terms. Find the output after coherent detection with a local carrier of amplitude 1 V and zero phase error.
steps: Message: m(t) = 2 cos(2π × 1000t) V. Carrier: A_c = 10 V, f_c = 100000 Hz.
DSB-SC wave: s(t) = 10 × 2 cos(2π1000t) cos(2π100000t) = 20 cos(2π1000t) cos(2π100000t) V.
Use 20 cos A cos B = 10[cos(A − B) + cos(A + B)]. Lower sideband: 10 cos(2π(100000 − 1000)t) = 10 cos(2π99000t) V. Upper sideband: 10 cos(2π(100000 + 1000)t) = 10 cos(2π101000t) V.
So the sidebands are 10 V peak at 99 kHz and 10 V peak at 101 kHz.
Coherent detector output amplitude: (A_c A_lo/2) × A_m = (10 × 1/2) × 2 = 10 V. Output: 10 cos(2π1000t) V.
examples.answer: The sidebands are 10 V peak at 99 kHz and 10 V peak at 101 kHz; coherent detection with a 1 V local carrier gives 10 cos(2π1000t) V, a 10 V peak 1 kHz tone.

traps: DSB-SC is not plain AM with a smaller carrier: the carrier is zero, so the envelope is |m(t)| and an envelope detector gives distortion.
A 90° phase error gives zero output, not half output. Half output comes from a 60° phase error, because cos 60° = 0.5.
Do not draw a spectral line at f_c. For a tone the only lines are at f_c − f_m and f_c + f_m.
DSB-SC bandwidth is 2W, not W. The one-sideband case in Chapter 2.3 has bandwidth W.
A frequency error gives a beat factor cos(2πΔf t), not a fixed attenuation. A phase error gives a fixed cos φ factor.

quiz.q: Write the time-domain expression for a DSB-SC wave and name every symbol.
quiz.a: s(t) = A_c m(t) cos(2πf_c t), where A_c is the carrier amplitude in volts, m(t) is the message voltage, and f_c is the carrier frequency in hertz.

quiz.q: Why does the DSB-SC spectrum have no carrier line at f_c?
quiz.a: The transmitted wave is A_c m(t) cos(2πf_c t). Multiplication shifts the message spectrum to f_c − W to f_c + W but adds no separate carrier term. So the Fourier transform has no impulse at ±f_c.

quiz.q: A 4 V peak, 2 kHz tone modulates a 20 V peak, 500 kHz carrier in DSB-SC. Find the sideband frequencies and amplitudes.
quiz.a: Sideband amplitude is A_c A_m/2 = 20 × 4/2 = 40 V. Frequencies are 500 − 2 = 498 kHz and 500 + 2 = 502 kHz. Each sideband is 40 V peak.

quiz.q: A coherent detector has a local carrier with 60° phase error. What is the output relative to zero phase error?
quiz.a: The output scales by cos φ. cos 60° = 0.5, so the output is half the zero-error output.

quiz.q: A DSB-SC signal is received with no phase error but a local oscillator frequency error of 5 Hz. What happens to the recovered message?
quiz.a: The low-pass output is multiplied by cos(2π × 5t). For a 1 kHz tone message this gives tones at 995 Hz and 1005 Hz, a beat. The message is not recovered cleanly.

quiz.q: State the output of a coherent detector for local carrier amplitude A_lo and phase error φ.
quiz.a: y(t) = (A_c A_lo/2) m(t) cos φ, where A_c is the received carrier amplitude and m(t) is the message.

quiz.q: Why is a pilot tone useful in DSB-SC reception?
quiz.a: A small pilot tone at f_c gives the receiver a reference for frequency and phase. The receiver filters and uses it to lock its local oscillator, so coherent detection remains synchronized.

quiz.q: Compare DSB-SC with plain AM for the same message and carrier amplitude, in terms of transmitted power and receiver complexity.
quiz.a: DSB-SC removes the carrier, so it does not waste carrier power; for the same sideband amplitude it needs less total power than AM. Its receiver needs carrier recovery and coherent detection, so it is more complex than the envelope detector used for plain AM.

beyond: Not for the exam. BPSK is mathematically DSB-SC with a bipolar message, so carrier recovery loops such as the Costas loop return in digital passband systems. Quadrature modulation sends two DSB-SC waves on the same carrier with a 90° phase difference. Software-defined radios implement the product and low-pass filter in digital signal processing after sampling. Search next for carrier recovery, Costas loop, pilot-aided synchronization and quadrature amplitude modulation.
